In Frosthaven, the recommended scenario level is calculated as:

> the average level of the characters divided by 2 (rounded up)

For example, if all characters are level 2, the average level (2) divided by 2 equals 1, so the scenario is still level 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase.

However, at the start of any scenario, you can set the scenario level to any number from 0–7, regardless of this recommendation. You can decrease it if your party is struggling or increase it to keep the game challenging as your party grows stronger.

In Frosthaven, here's how **advantage** works with attack modifier cards:

With **advantage**, the attacker draws **two modifiers** and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

**Handling rolling modifiers:** If the first draw is a *rolling modifier*, the attacker continues drawing modifiers one at a time until a non-rolling modifier is drawn, then draws one more modifier and ignores any rolling icon on it. The attacker then uses all the initial rolling modifiers plus whichever of the last two modifiers they choose (the better one for monsters, either one for characters).

If the first draw is not a rolling modifier but the second draw is, the rolling icon on the second modifier is still ignored.

**Ambiguous modifiers:** When comparing modifiers with non-numeric effects (like elemental infusions or negative conditions), any non-numeric effect is considered to have a positive but undefined value. If there is ambiguity about which is better, the attacker must use the one drawn first.

**Stacking:** An attack cannot gain multiple instances of **advantage** or **disadvantage**. If an attack has both, it is considered to have neither.

In Frosthaven, *Poison* does the following:

In other words, a poisoned figure takes increased damage from attacks against it, and if healed while poisoned, the healing removes the *Poison* condition but does **not** restore any hit points.

In Frosthaven, **looting** refers to the act of collecting loot tokens and treasure tiles from the map.

*Loot X* is an ability that allows a figure to loot all loot tokens and treasure tiles within range X, including any in their current hex. This ability is unaffected by the presence of figures or overlay tiles, and it cannot be performed if there are no loot tokens or treasure tiles within the specified range.

When a loot token is looted, it is removed from the map. If the looting figure is a **monster**, nothing else happens. If the looting figure is a **character**, they draw one card from the loot deck (unless it is empty). 

- If the loot card provides a random item, the character checks off *T* (x1) in the scenario entry's loot table, then draws one card from the random item deck and adds it to their pool of items immediately.
- If the loot card provides money or resources, the character does not gain them until the end of the scenario.

Characters must also **loot any loot tokens or treasure tiles present in their hex at the end of their turn** (end-of-turn looting). No figures besides characters perform end-of-turn looting.

When a treasure tile is looted, it is removed from the map. Monsters cannot loot treasure tiles.

In Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), *advantage* works with attack modifier cards as follows:

> With **advantage**, the attacker draws two modifiers and uses one of them. A monster always uses the better one, but a character may use either one.

**Special handling for rolling modifiers:**

If the first draw is a rolling modifier, you keep drawing additional modifiers one at a time until you get a non-rolling modifier. Then you draw **one more** modifier and ignore any rolling icon on it.

You then compare the first non-rolling modifier with the final one drawn. With *advantage*, you use all the initial rolling modifiers plus **whichever of the last two modifiers you choose** (characters pick the better one; monsters always do).

**Additional rules:**

- If the second draw is a rolling modifier but the first is not, the rolling icon on the second modifier is still ignored.
- An attack cannot have multiple instances of *advantage* or *disadvantage*. If an attack has both, it has neither.
- Any ranged attack on an adjacent enemy automatically gains *disadvantage*.

In Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), **Studded Leather** (item #014) is a body slot item that costs 20 gold.

**Effect:** When you are attacked, before drawing an attack modifier card, the attacker gains *disadvantage* on the attack and you gain *Shield 1* for the attack.

The item is *spent* after use.

In Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), according to the FAQ:

> If a Null (x0) is included in the final attack modifier draws, no matter where, the final damage will always be 0. If you draw a x2, it can be inserted at any time during attack modification including at the very end. (For example, if I have an Attack 3, draw a rolling +1, and finally a x2, I can decide if my final damage is 7 (3x2) + 1 or 8 (3+1) x2.)

**In short:** With a *Null*, your damage is always 0 regardless of order. With a *x2*, you choose when to apply it—even after all other rolling modifiers are resolved.

In Gloomhaven (2nd Edition), the recommended scenario level is calculated by taking the **average level of all characters, dividing by 2, and rounding up**.

For example, if all characters are level 2, the average is 2 ÷ 2 = 1, so the scenario level remains 1. Only once a character reaches level 3 would the scenario level potentially increase to 2.

However, at the start of any scenario, you can set the level to any number from 0–7, regardless of the recommendation. You can decrease it if your party is struggling or increase it to maintain challenge as your party grows stronger. (Rulebook)
